sections.section_title: The First Seal -- The White Horse
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies the first horseman as a figure on a white horse carrying a bow, given a crown (divine passive), and going out conquering, with the document's color-coding and vocabulary placing this rider under divine authorization as an agent of conquest dispatched by the Lamb's seal-opening and the living creature's command.

sections.section_title: The Second Seal -- The Red Horse
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies the red horse's rider as granted authority (divine passive) to take peace from the earth, causing mutual slaughter with the verb sphazo (the same word used of the Lamb's own death), with the great sword representing divine permission for warfare as an instrument of judgment within the prophetic covenant-curse tradition (Leviticus 26:25; Ezekiel 14:21).

sections.section_title: The Third Seal -- The Black Horse
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the black horse's rider with scales representing famine conditions -- grain at ruinous prices (a full day's wage for one person's daily ration) -- with the command not to damage oil and wine indicating either restrained, partial judgment or disproportionate economic impact on the poor, within the prophetic tradition of famine as covenant judgment (Leviticus 26:26; Ezekiel 4:16).

sections.section_title: The Fourth Seal -- The Pale Horse
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies the pale horse's rider as Death personified, with Hades following, given authority (divine passive) over a fourth of the earth to kill by sword, famine, pestilence, and wild beasts -- corresponding directly to Ezekiel 14:21's four acts of divine judgment, with scope explicitly limited to a quarter of the earth as preliminary rather than final judgment.

sections.section_title: The Fifth Seal -- The Souls Under the Altar
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the fifth seal reveals the souls of those slain 'because of the word of God and the testimony they had maintained,' located under the heavenly altar where sacrificial blood was poured, sharing the Lamb's own verb (esphagmenon), given white robes as vindication, and told to rest until the full number of fellow servants yet to be killed is completed.
sections.relevance: The vindication (white robes) is given specifically to those who 'maintained' (eichon) their testimony and who were slain for the word of God -- those whose faithfulness extended to death. The white robes correspond to the conqueror's reward promised in Sardis (3:5). The neutral reading states that the document 'promises that those who are killed for the word of God and the testimony will be vindicated, robed in white, and given rest.' The specificity of who receives vindication -- those who maintained the word and testimony to the point of death -- implies that the outcome depends on the maintenance of faithfulness rather than on initial entry into the community. The revelation that more servants 'are to be killed even as they had been' presents ongoing faithfulness unto death as the expected pattern for the community, not an anomaly.
key_phrases: slain because of the word of God
the testimony which they had maintained
rest for a little while longer
fellow servants and their brethren who were to be killed even as they had been

sections.section_title: The Sixth Seal -- Cosmic Upheaval and the Wrath of the Lamb
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the sixth seal as deploying the full prophetic Day of the LORD vocabulary -- earthquake, darkened sun, blood-red moon, falling stars, rolled-up sky, displaced mountains -- with every class of humanity (seven categories from kings to slaves) hiding from 'the wrath of the Lamb' and asking 'who is able to stand?', a question the neutral reading says is answered in chapter 7 by those whose faithfulness has prepared them.
sections.relevance: The question 'who is able to stand?' directly raises the issue of standing before God's judgment. The neutral reading explicitly states: 'The standing is not automatic or guaranteed to all; it belongs to those whose faithfulness, described in the language of the seven messages, has prepared them for this day.' It further concludes that the chapter's entire structure 'reinforces the conditional and urgent nature of the assemblies' situation: the outcome is determined by present faithfulness, not by past status or external identity.' The seven social categories encompassing all ranks demonstrate that no position or identity provides automatic exemption from judgment. The answer (deferred to chapter 7) identifies those who can stand as those who 'wash their robes in the blood of the Lamb' and come through the great tribulation -- language of ongoing active faithfulness, not of a status conferred once and held irrevocably.
key_phrases: the great day of their wrath has come
hide us from the face of the one who sits on the throne
